title: Not tight-fisted, not wasteful
hook: don't chain your hand to your neck nor stretch it all the way out (17:29)
tomorrow: Don't follow what you don't know

segments.voice: Yesterday: birr al-walidayn, goodness to parents. Your line was not even a sigh.

Hold your hand up in front of you. Now pull it in tight and press your fist to your throat, as if it were tied there. That's one picture. Now fling it out, fingers wide, as far as your arm will reach, so anything you were holding falls through. That's the other. Surah seventeen uses both pictures, in one verse, to talk about money. Neither is the way. Today: what's in between.

The verses just before set the scene: give the relative his due, and the needy, and the traveler, and don't squander. That's tabdhir, from a root used for scattering seed. Then 17:29, in Pickthall's translation: "And let not thy hand be chained to thy neck nor open it with a complete opening, lest thou sit down rebuked, denuded." The chained hand is the miser: it can't reach anyone. The hand opened all the way is the opposite trouble: everything spills, and you sit down with nothing, blamed and stripped bare. The verse makes a hero of neither extreme. Another surah, Al-Furqan, describes the servants of the Merciful as people who, when they spend, are neither wasteful nor stingy, but take a stand between the two. A scene in Bukhari shows how the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ applied it. His companion Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas fell badly ill and wanted to leave all his wealth in charity. The Prophet said no. Half? No. A third? A third, the Prophet said, and a third is a lot. Better to leave your heirs well off than dependent on others. So generosity has a shape. It reaches out, and it keeps enough to carry the people who depend on you. Al-Isra's commands go on: after no sigh at your parents, a hand neither tied nor emptied.
screen: `TABDHIR: SEED SCATTERED CARELESSLY.` · `THE CHAINED HAND, THE SPILLING HAND.` · `SA'D: NOT ALL, NOT HALF. A THIRD.` · `GENEROSITY HAS A SHAPE.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE HAND.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open in your lap, palms up, not clenched and not stretched, and feel that middle position. Then think about your spending lately: one place your hand has been tied, holding back from someone in need, and one place it's been flung open with no thought. Don't judge it; just notice which side you lean toward.
Not tight-fisted, and not wasteful either: a hand neither chained to the neck nor flung all the way open. Today's word.
Your line: the middle hand. Not chained, and not spilling. Rest well.

howItsDone: Muslim teaching on money draws on 17:26–29 and 25:67 to call for moderation between stinginess and waste; Islamic law limits bequests to a third of an estate, following the hadith of Sa'd.

chat.says: What does Surah seventeen say about how to spend money?
options: Neither a hand chained to your neck nor one flung wide open: the middle way.
Mostly avoid waste; holding tightly to your money is never the problem.
Keep your wealth for yourself first; giving can wait until you're rich.
chat.meaning: 17:29 warns against both: the chained hand can't reach anyone, and the hand opened all the way spills everything.
